survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study pools OECD PISA 2009 and 2015 reading data and estimates four-level linear probability models with students nested in schools, nested in country-years, nested in countries. Because PISA uses complex sampling procedures, the authors weight all analyses by normalized student weights so that each country contributes equally regardless of its student population size. They do not use BRR/Fay’s method replicate weights; instead they rely on cluster-robust standard errors with clustering at the country, country-year, and school levels. The paper also reports robustness checks using logit models with the same weights, indicating that the weighting strategy is consistently applied across specifications.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample is restricted to OECD countries. Countries were excluded if country-level information was unavailable and if they had fewer than 40 immigrant students (first or second generation) in the sample; this led to excluding Japan, Korea, Poland, and Turkey. At the student level, observations with missing values on any variable were excluded using listwise deletion. The final dataset contains 422,172 students in 12,255 schools across 54 country-years in 30 countries, pooled from PISA 2009 and PISA 2015.

main_findings.target_variable: Low reading performance (below PISA reading proficiency level 2)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Four-level LPM (weighted by normalized student weights; estimates averaged over five plausible values). Public posting: b = -0.158 (s.e. = 0.067), Model 5; interaction with first generation: b = -0.160 (s.e. = 0.036), b = -0.124 (s.e. = 0.029) for second generation. Achievement data to authorities: b = 0.029 (s.e. = 0.101), Model 7; interaction with first generation: b = -0.179 (s.e. = 0.055), interaction with second generation: b = -0.125 (s.e. = 0.049). Standardized testing alone: not statistically significant (Model 3/4).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 & 2015 Reading the study leveraged public posting of achievement data and immigrant status (first- and second-generation) to predict low reading performance (below proficiency level 2), finding that public provision of aggregated achievement data was associated with a reduced probability of low reading performance for all students and especially for first-generation immigrants. This indicates that accountability mechanisms that make assessment results publicly visible may be more effective than standardized testing alone for reducing low reading risks among immigrant students, though the design is observational and cannot establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses OECD PISA 2009 and 2015 reading data for 15-year-olds pooled across 30 OECD countries (422,172 students) to model the risk of low reading performance, defined as scoring below PISA reading proficiency level 2 (dummy created from the first five plausible values and averaged across five models). The authors estimate four-level linear probability models with students nested in schools, country-years, and countries, using normalized student weights and cluster-robust standard errors (clustering at country, country-year, and school). They find that standardized testing alone (regular mandatory tests) is not statistically significant, while making aggregated achievement data publicly available is associated with lower risk of low reading performance (b = −0.158, s.e. = 0.067), with stronger negative interactions for first-generation immigrants (b = −0.160, s.e. = 0.036). Providing achievement data to administrative authorities shows smaller and less robust effects. Limitations include only two waves for longitudinal country fixed effects and potential residual time-varying confounding.
